title: Who are you? Shankara at the cave
hookLine: a teacher asks a boy who he is
carry: avidya: taking what you see for who you are
tomorrow: a sage who has read everything comes to a teacher in sorrow. why?

lines: NOT EARTH. NOT WATER. NOT THE MIND.
cards: Shankara's traditional life stories say he left home as a boy to find a teacher, and walked a long way to the banks of the Narmada river. There, in a cave, sat the sage Govindapada.

The old man asked what any teacher asks a new student: who are you? The boy could have given his name, his village, his family. Instead, the tradition says, he answered in verses that turn down every label.
I am not earth, not water, not fire, not air, not space, not the senses, not the mind. What remains is the one alone, Shiva, the auspicious, and that I am. Govindapada took him on.
Years later, Shankara opened his great commentary on the Brahma Sutras by explaining why that question is so hard to answer.

teach.b: Before the first sutra, he writes a preface on adhyasa, superimposition. In paraphrase: the subject, the one who says I, and the object, whatever can be called this, are as opposed as light and darkness.
Yet people mix them all the time, the way mother-of-pearl glints on a beach and is taken for silver. I am this body. I am tired.
This is mine. The wise call the mix-up avidya, not-knowing, and telling the self from what's laid over it, vidya. That's jnana for Shankara: not collecting facts, but the shell seen as a shell.
It's what the boy at the cave did: set aside everything that can be seen, to point at the one who sees. A neighbor tradition says something close.

Paul, in a letter in the Christian Bible, writes in the King James Version: "For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known."
What they share: ordinary seeing is partial, and a clearer seeing is possible.

teach.h: FACE TO FACE, OR NEVER OTHER.
teach.b: The honest difference: Paul looks ahead to meeting God face to face, two who know each other.

teach.h: JNANA: THE SHELL IS JUST A SHELL.
teach.b: For Shankara, when the mix-up lifts, the self is known as never other than Brahman. Other Vedanta teachers, Ramanuja and Madhva among them, read these sutras differently. This week follows Shankara.

how: In Advaita Vedanta, students read the Brahma Sutras with Shankara's commentary under a teacher and reflect on the difference between the self and what is not the self; verses attributed to Shankara that say 'I am not this' are still recited. Christians read Paul's words in 1 Corinthians 13 as a hope of seeing God face to face.

games.q: Shankara says the one who says I and the things it sees are as opposed as light and dark. so why does anyone say 'I am this body'?
o: a mix-up he calls adhyasa, laying one over the other.
because the body really is the self, so there's no mistake.
because the sutras tell people to say it.
games.why: Shankara calls it superimposition, like silver seen on a shell. The wise name it avidya, not-knowing; telling them apart is vidya.

practice: Look at one object near you, a cup, a key, a leaf, and take in its color and its edges. Then ask the boy's question, quietly: who is seeing this?
Let the object and the noticing rest side by side without naming either, and when a label slides in, let it slide back out.

wordCard.voice: Jnana: knowledge, in Shankara's sense. Not gathering facts, but seeing through the mix-up of self and not-self.

orig.note: Sanskrit jnana, knowledge; for Shankara, the knowing that sees through the mix-up of self and not-self.

carryVoice: Your line: avidya is taking what you see for who you are. The shell was never silver. Day one of the sutras, done.

sources.ref: Shankara, Brahma Sutra Bhashya, introduction (adhyasa bhashya): subject and object opposed as light and darkness; superimposition defined; shell and silver, one moon as two; called avidya; its removal is vidya; all dealings presuppose it
